what: One licensed Texas child care center's published family handbook (85-page PDF, about 30,600 words), checked at Standard effort. The center isn't named and no handbook text is published; each finding was read against the rule by hand (not by a lawyer).

findings.requirement: Parents may visit the center during hours of operation without prior approval to observe their child and program.
findings.why: The handbook lets staff deny entry to a parent who poses a risk; the rule lists no exception, but a safety exception is common sense.

findings.requirement: If the center does not carry required liability insurance, parents must be notified in writing before admission.
findings.verdict: depends on facts outside the handbook
findings.why: The handbook says the center (a state agency) can't buy insurance coverage; if it carries no liability insurance, parents must be told in writing before admission, which could be a separate form.

findings.requirement: If applicable, the handbook must state transportation and water activity procedures.
findings.why: Swim lessons and splash days are described, but there is no clear transportation or water-activity procedure section.

findings.requirement: The handbook must state parent rights consistent with Division 5 of Subchapter B.
findings.why: Flagged as check by hand; the handbook has a short parent-rights section worth comparing with the full list of rights.

findings.requirement: Children's records must be immediately accessible to caregivers during hours of operation for emergency use.
findings.verdict: depends on facts outside the handbook
findings.why: Records 'locked in an administrator's office' may not be immediately accessible to caregivers in an emergency, as the rule requires.

findings.requirement: A food allergy emergency plan is required for each child with a health-care-professional-diagnosed food allergy.
findings.why: The rule requires the plan to be signed and dated by the child's health-care professional and parent; the handbook's allergy policy doesn't say so.
The quoted rule is about keeping immunization records, including exemptions; it doesn't require admitting unvaccinated children.
